Overtime 
Occasionally, we may need you to work more than your regular working hours. We will 
pay for overtime work according to local and national laws. [Insert this if employees are in the U.S: If you are an exempt employee, you are not 
entitled to overtime pay by federal law. In the event that an exempt employee must work 
overtime, we will set a cap for overtime hours at [10 hours per week] to prevent 
overworking and burnout. If you are a non-exempt employee, you are entitled to overtime

If you are a non-exempt employee, you will receive your regular hourly rate with a 
premium for working on a holiday.

Compensation status 
[Insert this section if you are covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) in the 
U.S.] 
 
There are two types of employees under FLSA guidelines: 
 
■ Non-exempt employees, who are covered by the FLSA’s minimum wage and 
overtime provisions. ■ Exempt employees, who aren’t covered by the FLSA because they meet three 
exemption criteria: (a) they are paid at least [$23,600] per year ([$455] per week), 
(b) they are paid on a salary basis, and (c) they perform exempt job

Holiday pay 
■ Exempt employees are entitled to their normal compensation without any 
deductions. ■ Permanent non-exempt employees receive holiday pay as a benefit after they 
have worked with us for more than [three months.] Working on a holiday 
These holidays are considered “off-days” for most employees. If you need a team 
member to work on a holiday, inform them at least [three days] in advance.

We [will/ won’t] count hours you worked on a holiday to decide whether you are entitled 
to overtime pay.

Please record your overtime hours accurately, so we can calculate 
your pay correctly. We also ask you to work overtime only after it’s authorized by your 
supervisor to make our record-keeping easier.]

Remote working 
Remote working refers to working from a non-office location on a temporary or 
permanent basis. If you’re an office-based employee, you may work remotely for a maximum of [two 
consecutive weeks] per year. You may arrange this if you [are a new parent or suffer 
from a short-term disability.] If you have another reason, talk to your manager. Submit 
your remote working requests [through our HRIS] at least [one week] in advance.

Most employees must meet all 
three criteria to be exempt. If you are unsure as to whether you should be exempt or not, please ask HR to clarify 
your status. The FLSA excludes some types of jobs (e.g. railroad workers, truck drivers) because 
they are covered by other federal laws. Some other workers, like outside salespeople, 
are excluded by definition. Feel free to ask HR for clarifications any time.

Workers’ compensation 
We strive to keep our workplace safe, but accidents may happen occasionally. Employees who are injured at work (by accident or disease) can receive wage 
replacement, medical care and rehabilitation benefits according to workers’ 
compensation laws, when appropriate. Please inform us of your injury as soon as 
possible.

Performance management 
We have built our performance management practices to: 
■ Ensure you understand your job responsibilities and have specific goals to meet. ■ Provide you with actionable and timely feedback on your work. ■ Invest in development opportunities that help you grow professionally. ■ Recognize and reward your work in financial or non-financial ways (e.g. employee awards.)

There's no single universal standard, but here's how it typically breaks down by region and context:

**United States**  
- The traditional full-time benchmark is **40 hours per week**, a norm rooted in the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) and widely adopted by employers.  
- The **Affordable Care Act (ACA)** legally defines full-time as **30 or more hours per week** for the purpose of employer-provided health insurance mandates (the "shared responsibility" penalty).  
- The FLSA itself doesn't define "full-time" or "part-time"; that's left to employers, which is why you'll see company policies range from 30 to 40 hours.  
- Many organizations use 37.5 or 38 hours as a "standard" workweek to account for unpaid lunch breaks, but 40 remains the most common threshold for benefits, overtime calculations, and salary classification.

**Europe & Other Regions**  
- The **European Union** averages around **38–40 hours** per week, though many countries fall below 38. For example, France's legal max is 35 hours (though overtime and exceptions are common), and Germany typically averages **38–39 hours** per collective bargaining agreements.  
- **UK**: No statutory minimum for full-time, but 35–40 hours is standard, with many contracts settling at 37.5.  
- **Canada & Australia**: Most commonly **37.5–40 hours**, with provincial/territorial labor standards influencing overtime and part-time thresholds.

**Key Variables**  
- **Industry**: Tech, consulting, and finance often expect 40+ with "flexible" or "expected" overtime. Unionized or public-sector roles more frequently cap full-time at 35–38.  
- **Employment type**: Salaried vs. hourly, contract vs. permanent, and whether the role is exempt (no overtime pay) or non-exempt (overtime eligible) all affect how hours are tracked and what "full-time" means functionally.  
- **Company policy**: Many employers define full-time in employee handbooks (e.g., "30+ hours = eligible for PTO," "40+ = overtime eligible").

Bottom line: If you're asking for legal compliance, **30 hours/week** is the ACA threshold in the U.S., but **40 hours/week** is the de facto full-time standard. Outside the U.S., expect **35–40**, depending on the country and sector. Always check the specific employer's handbook or local labor code for the exact definition applicable to a given role.

Employment contracts for full-time and part-time workers vary significantly depending on the country, state or province, industry, and company policy. Below is a detailed breakdown of the most common contract types you'll encounter globally, along with the key variables that shape them.

### 🧑‍💼 Full-Time Employee Contracts
| Contract Type | Typical Structure | Key Features |
|--------------|-------------------|------------|
| **Permanent / Open-Ended** | No fixed end date; ongoing employment | Standard hours (usually 35–40 hrs/week); full benefit eligibility; standard statutory notice periods for termination; most common globally |
| **Fixed-Term** | Start and end date clearly specified | Used for projects, seasonal work, or backfilling parental/medical leave. In many jurisdictions, after 2–4 renewals or a certain duration, the contract automatically converts to permanent. |
| **Contract-to-Hire / Probationary** | Trial period (typically 3–12 months) before permanent offer | Employer evaluates fit; may offer reduced or pro-rated benefits during probation. If the probation is passed, the employee transitions to a permanent contract. |
| **Executive / Specialized** | Custom-drafted with specific clauses | Often includes bonus structures, stock options, longer notice periods, confidentiality/non-compete clauses, and tailored termination terms. |

### 🧑‍💼 Part-Time Employee Contracts
| Contract Type | Typical Structure | Key Features |
|--------------|-------------------|------------|
| **Permanent Part-Time** | Ongoing, reduced hours (e.g., 20 hrs/week) | Entitled to pro-rated benefits, holiday pay, and similar legal protections as full-time staff, though exact rules depend heavily on local law. |
| **Fixed-Term Part-Time** | Fixed duration with fewer hours | Same conversion rules as fixed-term full-time, but applied to a part-time baseline. Common in seasonal retail, education support, or project-based reduced-hours roles. |
| **Casual / On-Call** | Hours vary week to week; no guaranteed minimum | May come with "casual loading" (a higher hourly rate instead of paid leave/sick days), or in some regions, entitlements accrue after a threshold of hours worked (e.g., 25+ hrs/week for 12+ weeks). |
| **Zero-Hours** | No guaranteed hours; worker called in as needed | Highly regulated or banned in some jurisdictions (e.g., UK restrictions on exclusivity clauses, Australia's "casual conversion" rules). Used in hospitality, retail, on-call medical/emergency services, and gig-adjacent roles. |
| **Job-Sharing** | Two part-time employees split one full-time role | Often includes shared responsibilities, pro-rated pay, and joint or separate benefit enrollment depending on company policy and local law. |

### 🔍 Key Variables That Shape the Contract
- **Hours threshold**: What defines "full-time" vs. "part-time" varies (e.g., 30 hrs/week in some US contexts, 35 in EU, 38 in Australia).
- **Benefit eligibility**: Full-time = typically full benefits; part-time = often pro-rated, conditional, or subject to a minimum hours threshold.
- **Termination notice**: Legally mandated based on tenure, contract type, and jurisdiction (e.g., 1 week per year of service in many places, with caps or floors).
- **Contract conversion / permanence**: Many regions have "permanence clauses" or "right to request" rules that allow casual/part-time workers to convert to permanent status after meeting hour/tenure criteria.
- **Jurisdiction**: 
  - *US*: Mostly "at-will" employment, but contracts still define pay, benefits, severance, and confidentiality. State laws (e.g., California, New York) add predictive scheduling, part-time protections, and conversion rules.
  - *EU*: Stronger statutory protections, mandatory written terms, strict fixed-term limits, and automatic conversion after set periods.
  - *Australia*: Governed by the Fair Work Act; casual conversion rights, minimum engagement periods, and clear distinction between casual, part-time, and full-time.

### ⚖️ Important Disclaimer
Employment law is highly localized. If you're drafting, reviewing, or asking about specific rights in a particular country, state, or industry, I strongly recommend consulting the local labor code, a qualified HR professional, or an employment lawyer. Many jurisdictions have mandatory minimum terms, benefit thresholds, and specific rules about contract conversion, especially for fixed-term or casual work.

### 🧑‍💼 Part-Time Employee Contracts
| Contract Type | Typical Structure | Key Features |
|--------------|-------------------|------------|
| **Permanent Part-Time** | Ongoing, reduced hours (e.g., 20 hrs/week) | Entitled to pro-rated benefits, holiday pay, and similar legal protections as full-time staff, though exact rules depend heavily on local law. |

| **Casual / On-Call** | Hours vary week to week; no guaranteed minimum | May come with "casual loading" (a higher hourly rate instead of paid leave/sick days), or in some regions, entitlements accrue after a threshold of hours worked (e.g., 25+ hrs/week for 12+ weeks). |

- **Termination notice**: Legally mandated based on tenure, contract type, and jurisdiction (e.g., 1 week per year of service in many places, with caps or floors).
- **Contract conversion / permanence**: Many regions have "permanence clauses" or "right to request" rules that allow casual/part-time workers to convert to permanent status after meeting hour/tenure criteria.

Employment contract types vary significantly depending on country, region, industry, and employer policy, but here are the most common structures for full-time and part-time employees across many jurisdictions:

### 🔹 Full-Time Employee Contracts
| Contract Type | Typical Duration | Hours/Week | Key Features |
|--------------|------------------|------------|--------------|
| **Permanent/Open-Ended** | Indefinite | 35–40 (varies by role/region) | Most common; includes full benefits (health, retirement, paid leave); subject to standard termination/notice periods |
| **Fixed-Term** | Specific end date or completion of a project | Usually full-time hours | Used for temporary coverage, seasonality, or project work; ends automatically on the date/event; may offer pro-rated benefits; some regions allow conversion to permanent after repeated renewals |
| **Fixed-Duration / Seasonal** | Tied to a season or campaign | Full-time hours during peak period | Common in retail, agriculture, hospitality; often renewed annually or not at all |
| **Probationary** | Introductory period (3–6 months) | Full-time hours | Used to assess fit; may have shorter notice periods or reduced benefits initially, but often converts to permanent upon successful completion |
| **Apprenticeship/Traineeship** | Fixed training period (1–4 years) | Combines work + study | Structured learning contract; often includes a wage scale that increases with skill milestones |

### 🔹 Part-Time Employee Contracts
| Contract Type | Typical Duration | Hours/Week | Key Features |
|--------------|------------------|------------|--------------|
| **Permanent Part-Time** | Indefinite | <35 (often 16–30) | Same pro-rated benefits as full-time permanent staff (prorated by hours); guaranteed minimum hours per contract or law |
| **Fixed-Term Part-Time** | End date or project | <35 | Same structure as fixed-term full-time, but hours are reduced; benefits pro-rated |
| **Job-Share** | Indefinite or fixed | Two people split one full-time role | Each party has a part-time contract; benefits and responsibilities are divided (or shared) per agreement |
| **Reduced-Hours / Flexible-Time** | Indefinite | Variable, agreed upon | May include compressed hours, flexible start/end times, or annualized hours (where total hours are spread across the year) |
| **Zero-Hours** | No guaranteed minimum | Variable, often on-call | Legality varies widely; in some regions, employers must offer a minimum number of hours or pay a guarantee; often criticized for instability |
| **Casual** | As-needed | Highly variable | May not guarantee regular hours; in some jurisdictions comes with a "casual loading" (extra pay instead of benefits like sick leave or vacation; in others, casuals have limited entitlements after a certain period |

### 🔹 Other Work Arrangements (Often Confused with Employee Contracts)
- **Independent Contractors/Freelancers**: Not "employees" under most labor laws; set their own rates, hours, and taxes; typically provide their own tools/insurance
- **Agency/Temporary Workers**: Employed by a staffing agency and assigned to a client; contract may be with the agency, not the host employer
- **Interns/Co-op Students**: May be paid, unpaid, or for credit; governed by education/training frameworks rather than standard employment law in many places

### ⚖️ Key Variables That Change the Contract
- **Minimum guaranteed hours**: Some regions legally require a minimum number of hours or pay if a shift is canceled last-minute
- **Benefits proration**: Part-time staff often get vacation, sick leave, and retirement contributions calculated as a percentage of full-time equivalents
- **Termination notice**: Permanent contracts usually require 1–4 weeks' notice (or pay in lieu); fixed-term contracts end on the date specified unless early termination clauses exist
- **Conversion rights**: After a certain number of renewals or months/years on a fixed-term or casual contract, some jurisdictions automatically grant permanent status

### 🌍 Jurisdictional Note
Contract structures are heavily shaped by local labor codes. For example:
- **EU**: Strong protections for fixed-term contracts; after 2–4 renewals, they often convert to permanent
- **UK**: "Zero-hours" contracts are legal but come with statutory rights after 12 weeks; part-time workers must not be treated less favorably on a pro-rata basis
- **US**: Contract types are more employer-driven; "at-will" employment is default in most states, meaning permanent contracts can be terminated by either party with proper notice (or none, depending on state), and benefits are not legally required to be pro-rated unless specified by company policy or a collective bargaining agreement
- **Australia**: National Employment Standards guarantee minimum hours, pro-rata leave for part-timers, and clear rules on casual conversion after 12 months

### 💡 Bottom Line
If you're drafting, reviewing, or transitioning between contracts, the most important steps are:
1. **Check the specific labor laws** of your country, state, or province
2. **Clarify hours, benefit eligibility, notice periods, and conversion/renewal terms** in writing
3. **Consult an HR professional or employment lawyer** for role- or region-specific guidance
